column2: [Gautama] "Where the Rathantara and the Brihat are sung, where the altar is strewn with white lotuses, where the soma-drinker comes with his bay horses, there I shall send you with this elephant.
I know you, slayer of Vritra, Shatakratu, who pass over all the worlds. If ever, by word or from attachment of mind, I have done you any wrong,
[Shakra] since I have followed this path of the people's world in the track of the elephant, may you, bowed before, instruct me; whatever you say, I shall do it all."

[Gautama] "The white female elephant and the young elephant, my son, that you took, whom I had ten years, who was my companion while I lived in the forest, give me that very elephant back, lord of the gods."
[Shakra] "Here is your son, the chief elephant of a chief of brahmins; he looks at you and smells you, and sniffs your feet with his trunk. Think of my welfare; salutations to you."
[Gautama] "May it always be well with you here, lord of the gods; I meditate on you and always offer worship. Give me also, Shakra, what is well; I accept the elephant given by you."
[Shakra] "Of the wise, the good and the great-souled, in whose hearts the Vedas are laid, you alone are such a one, great soul; I am awakened, and therefore I am pleased with you today.
Come, brahmin, quickly, with your son the elephant, and gain the blessed worlds at once and for a long time."
[Bhishma] Placing Gautama before him, with his son the elephant, the wielder of the thunderbolt crossed to heaven, hard to approach, together with the good.
What does the Grandsire know that is higher than the power of austerity? Tell me what is supreme above austerity.
[Bhishma] As long as people speak of austerity, Yudhishthira, so long it is for the worlds; but in my view, son of Kunti, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
On this too they cite an ancient tale: the dialogue between Bhagiratha and the great-souled Brahma.
Having passed beyond the world of the gods and the world of the cows, O Bharata, and the world of the sages, Bhagiratha came there, so it is heard.
Seeing him, Brahma spoke to King Bhagiratha: "How, Bhagiratha, have you come to this place, so hard to approach?
Neither gods nor gandharvas nor men, Bhagiratha, come here without austerities. How have you come here?"
[Bhagiratha] "I fearlessly gave food to brahmins, a hundred thousand times, and gave always; I held constantly the Brahmic vow. Know that I did not come here by the fruit of that.
Nor by the fruit of the ten eleven-night rites, the ten five-night rites, the eleven elevens, or the rites, or the hundred Jyotishtoma sacrifices I have offered.
In each of the Aptoryama rites I regularly gave ten, and gave milch cows, red cows, and Rohinis, and for that reason also.
I gave, O brahmin, ten times ten myriads of milk cows, yet I did not come by that.
I gave ten myriads of horses of the Bahlika breed, adorned with gold garlands, and yet did not come by that.
I gave eight crores of gold, O Brahma, ten in every sacrifice, and yet I did not come by the fruit of that.
Of dark-eared green horses, O Grandsire, I gave seventeen crores with gold garlands, O Brahma.
I gave seventeen thousand huge elephants with tusks like ploughshares, adorned with gold garlands, each with a mate.
Lord of the gods, I gave seventeen thousand golden-limbed chariots adorned with divine gold ornaments, yoked with well-adorned horses.
Of the sacrificial fees that the Vedas proclaim, I gave in ten Vajapeyas; yet by that too I have not come here.
By sacrifice and valour, equal in power to Shakra, I gave a thousand men wearing gold necklaces as sacrificial fee.
Having conquered all kings and sacrificed, O Grandsire, in eight Rajasuyas, I did not come by that.
O lord of the world, as long as the Ganga's stream flowed, the world was covered with my sacrificial fees, and I did not come by that.

Two thousand horses adorned with a hundred gold ornaments each, and a hundred choice villages, I gave in three parts to each; being an ascetic who eats by rule, restrained in speech, having taken up peace,
for a long time in the Himalaya, I bore on my head the Ganga's stream, so hard to bear, which Mahadeva held on his head. Not by that fruit either, Grandsire, have I come here.
The gods I worshipped with the shami throw, with ten thousands of one-day rites, with thirteens and twelve-day rites, and with the Paundarikas; yet not by their fruit.
Eight thousand white-humped bulls I gave to brahmins, each with a golden horn, and I gave their mates with gold necklaces.
I gave mountains of jewels heaped with gold and gems, and villages rich in wealth and grain by the hundred thousand.
Tirelessly I gave a hundred hundred milch cows to brahmins, having offered many great sacrifices; yet not by that.
I sacrificed with eleven-day rites with fees, with twelve-day rites, with Ashvamedhas, and with sixteen Arkayanas, O brahman; by their fruit I have not come here.
I gave a gold necklace to a single person, and a forest of golden trees and gem-adorned mango trees a yojana wide; yet I have not come by their fruit.
Without anger I kept the unassailable Turayana vow for thirty years, and day after day I gave brahmins a hundred cows and eight hundred more.
Milch cows and red cows, and likewise bulls, O lord of the world, I gave brahmins constantly, O lord of the gods; yet not by that fruit have I come here.
O brahman, I sacrificed to the thirty fires, and constantly, with eight Sarvamedhas and seven Naramedhas,
with ten Vishvajits and hundreds, eighteen more; yet not by their fruit, lord of the gods, have I come here.
On the Sarayu, the Bahuda, the Ganga and at Naimisha, I gave a myriad hundreds of cows; yet not by that.
What Indra hid in a cave, what Bhargava gained here by austerity, blazing here with Ushanas's brilliance, that choice thing I accomplished by a boon.
Then the brahmins were pleased when that rite was accomplished; there were a thousand sages gathered there, and they said to me, 'Go to Brahma's world,' O lord.
I was told so by a thousand pleased brahmins, O lord, and I came to this world; let there be no doubt about it here.
What was ordained by the Creator is as it is; but asked, I must speak truly: in my view there is no austerity higher than fasting. Salutations to you, best of gods; be gracious."
[Bhishma] To King Bhagiratha who had spoken so, Brahma paid honour, worthy of honour, by the rite seen in the rules.
By what does a man become long-lived, or short-lived? By what does he gain fame, or gain prosperity?
By austerity, by celibacy, by prayers, oblations and herbs, by birth or by conduct? Tell me that, Grandsire.
[Bhishma] I shall tell you on this what you ask me: by what a man becomes short-lived or long-lived,
by what he gains fame or prosperity, and how a man by his conduct is joined to what is best.
By conduct one gains long life, by conduct one gains prosperity, by conduct a man attains fame, in this world and after death.
A man of bad conduct does not gain great length of life here; beings fear him and so too they despise him.
Therefore he who desires his own well-being should practise right conduct here; conduct removes the bad marks even of a sinful body.
Dharma is marked by conduct, and the good are marked by conduct; the way the good live is the mark of conduct.
Even a man unseen, known only by report, who follows dharma and does works of prosperity, people hold dear.
Those who are unbelievers, inactive, who transgress teacher and scripture, ignorant of dharma and of bad conduct, become short-lived.
Men of bad character, who break bounds, who always mix in sexual union, are short-lived here and go to hell.
Even a man lacking all marks, if he has proper conduct, is faithful and free of envy, lives a hundred years.
One who is free of anger, truthful, harmless to beings, free of envy and straightforward, lives a hundred years.
The man who crushes clods, cuts grass, bites his nails, is always unclean from leavings and unsteady, does not gain long life.
He should wake in the Brahma muhurta, reflect on dharma and wealth, rise, rinse his mouth, and stand with folded hands for the morning twilight prayer.
In the same way he should attend the evening twilight, in silence. He should never gaze at the rising or the setting sun.
The sages gained long life through long twilight devotions; therefore he should always attend both twilights in silence.
A righteous king should make those twice-born who attend the morning twilight but not the evening one do a shudra's work.
He should never go to another man's wife, in any class. Nothing in the world shortens life like a man's resorting to another's wife.
Dressing the hair, applying collyrium, cleaning the teeth, and worshipping the gods he should do in the forenoon.
He should not look at faeces or urine, nor stand upon them; nor should he ever converse with a menstruating woman.
He should not pass faeces in a field or near a village; and never pass both urine and faeces in water.
He should always eat facing east, in silence, not disparaging the food; he should offer a portion mentally and, having eaten, touch fire.
Eating facing east gives long life, facing south, fame; eating facing west gives wealth, and eating facing north gives truth.
He should never sit on husks, hair, ashes or skulls, and should avoid from afar attending on another's seat.
He should perform pacifying oblations and have the Savitri rites performed; he may eat sitting, but never while walking.
He should not pass urine standing, nor on ashes, nor in a cow pen.
He should eat with wet feet but not go to bed with wet feet; eating with wet feet, he lives a hundred years.
When unclean from leavings, he should never touch the three radiant things: fire, a cow and a brahmin; so his life will not be harmed.
Unclean from leavings, he should never look at the three radiant things: the sun and moon, and the stars everywhere.
The vital breaths of a young man rise upward when an elder approaches; by rising and greeting he recovers them.
He should greet the aged, offer them a seat, wait on them with folded hands, and follow behind them as they go.
He should not sit on a broken seat and should avoid a broken bronze vessel; he should not eat in one garment, nor bathe naked, nor sleep naked, nor go to bed unclean from leavings.
Unclean, he should not touch the head, in which all the vital breaths rest; he should avoid pulling the hair and blows on the head.
He should never scratch the head with both hands, nor bathe the head too often; thus his life will not be harmed.
After bathing the head with oil he should not touch any other limb with it, nor eat sesame paste; so he gains long life.
Unclean, he should not teach nor ever study; in wind and foul smells he should not think of it even in mind.
On this the wise of old recite verses sung by Yama: "I cut off his life, and take his offspring."
The twice-born who recites the Veda while unclean, or through folly studies even in a time of no study, therefore even if diligent should never study when study is forbidden.
Those who urinate toward the sun, the wind, a cow or the twice-born, or on the road, become short-lived.
He should pass both urine and faeces facing north by day and facing south by night; so his life will not be harmed.
One who wishes to live long should not despise three slender things: a brahmin, a kshatriya and a snake; for all three are venomous.
An angry snake burns as far as it sees with its eye; a kshatriya, angered, burns as far as he touches with his might.
A brahmin destroys a family by meditation and a glance; therefore a wise man should serve these three with care.
One should never hold a feud against a teacher; an angry teacher, Yudhishthira, is to be honoured and appeased.
Whether he acts rightly or wrongly, one must behave well toward the teacher here; reviling the teacher burns away men's lives, without doubt.
One who wishes his own good should put urine far from the dwelling, foot-washing far, and the casting away of leavings far.
He should not travel too early, too late, or at noon, nor with strangers, nor alone, nor with low-born men.
Way should be given to a brahmin, to cows, to a king, to the old, to one carrying a burden, to a pregnant woman and to the weak.
He should circle trees known to him, and should circle all crossroads, keeping them to his right.
He should not resort to crossroads at noon, at night, at midnight, or at either twilight.
He should not wear shoes or clothes worn by others. He should always be a celibate student and not step on one foot with another.
On the new moon, the full moon, the fourteenth, and the eighth of every fortnight, he should always be a celibate.
He should not eat meat for no reason, nor eat it from behind; he should avoid abuse, slander and backbiting.
He should not be wounding, nor cruel in speech, nor take from a lowly man what is another's; he should not speak the harsh word by which another is distressed, which belongs to the sinful worlds.
Arrows of speech fly from the mouth; struck by them one grieves night and day. They strike another's vital places; the wise man does not loose them on others.
A forest pierced by arrows grows again, and one cut by an axe; but a wound of ill words, ugly, does not heal.
He should not mock the maimed, those with extra limbs, the unlearned, the aged, the poor or ugly, or the weak.
He should avoid unbelief, abuse of the Veda, contempt of the gods, hatred, stubbornness, arrogance and harshness.
He should not raise the rod against another, nor strike him down in anger; except for a son or a pupil, beating for instruction is held proper.
He should not speak ill of brahmins, nor point out the stars, nor mention the lunar day or fortnight; so his life will not be harmed.
After passing urine or faeces, or after walking on a road, he should wash his feet, and before study and before eating.
The gods ordained three purifiers for brahmins: what is unseen, what is cleansed by water, and what is praised by speech.
Samyava, krisara, meat, shashkuli and payasa should not be prepared for oneself, but be prepared for the gods.
He should always tend the fire, always give alms, always practise silence and the use of the tooth-stick, and should not be one over whom the sun rises while he sleeps; if so, he should do penance.
The mother should rise and greet the father first, or the teacher; so he gains long life.
He should avoid tooth-sticks that are always to be avoided, and use those seen in the scriptures, avoiding them on the parva days.
Facing north, he should always perform purification, attentive.
Without worshipping the gods he should never go to another, except to an old teacher, a righteous man or a wise one.
The very wise should not look at a dirty mirror, nor ever approach an unknown woman or a pregnant one.
He should not sleep with head to the north, nor to the west; the wise man should sleep with head to the east or the south.
He should not lie on a broken or cracked bed, nor with something between, nor with another, nor ever crosswise.
He should never bathe naked, nor at night; and having bathed, the very wise should not rub his limbs.
He should not anoint himself without bathing, nor shake out his clothes after bathing; a man should always wear damp garments, not drag a garland, nor wear it outside.
A red garland should not be worn; the wise wear white, excepting the lotus and the blue water-lily, O lord.
Red may be worn on the head, and also wild flowers; a golden garland never defiles. After bathing one should always apply moist unguent, O lord of the people.
A wise man should not wear his clothes inside out, nor wear what others have worn, nor a garment without a fringe.
One garment should be for the bed, O best of men, another for the roads, and another for the worship of the gods.
The wise man should anoint himself separately with priyangu and sandal, with bilva, with tagara and with saffron.
He should fast, bathed, pure and adorned; at all parva times he should always be celibate.
He should never eat what has been licked, nor what has had its essence removed, nor in front of those who watch without giving.
A wise man should not eat near another, nor when unclean, nor among the good; he should not eat from behind forbidden foods contrary to dharma.
A man who wishes well-being should not eat the pipal, the banyan, the hemp-leaf vegetable, or the udumbara.
He should avoid goat meat, beef and peacock; he should avoid dried meat, and what is stale.
A wise man should not take salt from his hand, nor eat curds and barley-meal at night; he should avoid meat without cause.
He should not eat in a pledged state nor at another's shraddha; he should eat attentively morning and evening, not between.
He should not eat in silence in one garment, nor unseated, nor ever on the ground, nor standing, nor with noise.
O lord of the people, he should give food first to guests with water, and then the wise man should eat, and not with his mind elsewhere.
Food to be shared in one row, O lord of men, he who eats without giving to his friends eats the Halahala poison.
Water, payasa, ghee, curds, barley-meal and honey, having set aside the remainder, should not be given to anyone.
While eating, O tiger among men, he should not entertain doubt; and one who seeks well-being should not drink curds as an after-drink.
Having rinsed his mouth, and let the water run off his hand, he should sprinkle the big toe of the right foot.
Placing his hand on his head and touching fire, attentive, a man skilled in practice gains pre-eminence among kinsmen.
Touching the vital breaths with water and the navel with the palm, he should stand touching, and not with a wet hand.
The part between the thumb is called the Brahma tirtha; behind the little finger is the Deva tirtha here.
With the middle of the thumb and forefinger, O Bharata, he should perform the ancestral rites, touching water properly.
He should not speak ill of others nor ever speak what is unpleasant; and one who seeks well-being should not stir up anger in anyone.
He should not wish to converse with the fallen and should avoid even seeing them; he should not associate, and so gains long life.
He should not go to a woman by day, nor to a maiden, nor to a harlot, nor to an unbathed woman; so he gains long life.
Having rinsed at his own tirtha when a rite is prepared, drinking three times and wiping twice, a man becomes purified.
Touching the senses once and sprinkling three times, a man should perform the ancestral and divine rites by the action seen in the Veda.
Hear from me, O Kaurava, also the purification for brahmins: having spoken what is proper and good, at the beginning and end of a meal,
in all purifications he should touch water with the Brahma tirtha; and after spitting or sneezing, touching water, he becomes pure.
An aged kinsman or a friend, even one who is poor, should be housed in the home; this brings wealth and long life.
Pigeons in the house bring wealth, as do parrots and mynas; these in houses are not for harm, nor are oil-drinkers.
Uddipakas, vultures, doves and bees, when they settle there, he should then perform a pacifying rite.
These are inauspicious, as is the cursing of great souls; the secrets of great souls should never be told.
He should not go to women forbidden, the wives of kings, nor friends' wives, nor those of physicians, children, the aged or servants, Yudhishthira.
Nor those of kinsmen, brahmins, or a refugee, nor of relatives, O king of kings; so he gains long life.
A house made by a brahmin and a builder, a wise man seeking well-being should always dwell in, O lord of men.
He should not sleep at twilight, O king, nor study, nor eat; the wise man so gains long life.
He should not perform ancestral rites by night, nor adorn himself after eating; one who desires prosperity should not draw water by night.
Barley-meal is always to be avoided at night, O Bharata, and the remains of food, white things, and water at a meal.
He should not overeat; he should not do so at night; he should not cut a twice-born's bond, and should not do it after eating.
O greatly wise one, one is fit to marry a maiden born of a great family, praised for her marks, and of fit age.
Having begotten offspring and established the family, sons should be given to learning and the family's duties, O Bharata.
A daughter, once born, should be given to a wise boy of good family; sons should be settled apart from the family, and servants may be obtained, O Bharata.
Having bathed his head, he should perform the divine and ancestral rites; not on the star of his birth, nor on Proshthapada, nor on the Agneya, O Bharata.
He should avoid all dreadful ones, and daily, and should avoid all that is declared in astrology.
Attentive, he should have his beard shaved facing east, or facing north, O king of kings; so he gains long life.
He should not speak ill of others or of himself; for abuse is not said to be for dharma, O best of the Bharatas.
He should avoid a deformed woman, and likewise a maiden, O best of men; one of the same sage lineage, and a deformed one, and one of his mother's own family.
He should avoid an aged woman, an ascetic, a devoted wife of another, one very dark, and one of a higher class.
The wise man should not go to one without a womb or of a wrong womb, nor to a tawny woman, nor to a leper woman; you should not marry such.
He should avoid one born in a family with epilepsy, a very low one, and one born in a family of those with white leprosy, O lord of men; of these three.
She who is endowed with marks and praised for them, pleasing and good to look at, you are fit to marry.
One should marry into a great family or an equal one, Yudhishthira; one who seeks well-being should not take a lower or a fallen one.
Having carefully kindled the fires, he should practise all the rites well ordained, as declared in the Vedas by brahmins.
He should not be jealous of women, and wives are to be guarded in every way; jealousy shortens life, so he should avoid it.
Sleeping by day shortens life, as do sleeping after sunrise, and sleeping in the morning and evening, and those who sleep unclean.
Adultery shortens life, as does the barber's leavings; these must be carefully avoided, and habit of them too, O Bharata.
At twilight he should not eat, bathe or pass faeces; he should be pure then and do nothing else.
He should honour brahmins after bathing, O lord of men, bow to the gods when bathed, and greet his teachers.
He should not go uninvited; a spectator may go to a sacrifice. Going uninvited shortens life, O Bharata.
He should not travel alone nor go at night. Before twilight has come, he should stay at home in the west.
The command of mother, father and teachers must be done; whether good or bad, it should not be weighed, O best of men.
Effort should be made in archery and the Veda, in riding on elephants and horses, and in the chariot's use. Be diligent, O king; the diligent prospers happily.
Unassailable by enemies, and in charge of servants and kinsmen and devoted to protecting subjects, he never suffers loss.
You should know the science of reasoning and of grammar, O Bharata, the science of the gandharvas, and the arts, O lord of men.
You should always hear the Purana, the histories, the tales, and the lives of great souls.
He should not approach his wife when she is menstruating, nor summon her; bathed on the fourth day, the wise man may go to her at night.
On the fifth day a woman is conceived, on the sixth a man; by this rule the wise man should approach his wife.
Kinsmen, relatives and friends should always be honoured, and he should sacrifice as he can with sacrifices of many fees; after that, O lord of men, the forest should be resorted to.
This is the account of the marks of long life told to you; the rest, Yudhishthira, you must take from the aged masters of the three Vedas.
Conduct brings prosperity, conduct increases fame; by conduct life grows, and conduct removes bad marks.
Of all the traditions, conduct is called best; dharma arises from conduct, and from dharma life increases.
This is conducive to fame, long life and heaven, a great blessing; Brahma declared it with compassion for all classes.
[Bhishma] Behave, dear child, like an elder, for you are always the eldest; and the conduct of a pupil toward a teacher, O Bharata, is weightier.
A pupil cannot behave toward a teacher who lacks understanding; the teacher's far-sightedness is the pupil's, O Bharata.
One may be blind in a blind hour, or a fool, or even wise; when there is an offence among them, he should speak of it by way of avoidance.
Openly, men with divided hearts may divide what has been made, O son of Kunti; enemies tormented by prosperity and wanting division do the same.
An eldest son increases a family or destroys it again; an eldest son who is born into a family may destroy it all.
If an elder brother wrongs his younger, he ceases to be the eldest, loses his share, and is to be restrained by kings.
A deceitful man undoubtedly goes to sinful worlds; his flower is like that of the vidula, and is said to be fruitless to his begetter.
Going there, as told, he of great fame placed a corpse at the city's gate, remembering Narada's words.
Give your father leave; it is the time for his austerity, and no anger, even slight, is in him, Yudhishthira.
Those two disciples of yours, Arjuna, ever dear and honoured, through their misdeed the Vrishnis have met destruction, O Partha.
Bhishma, of great splendour, attained the Vasus themselves; only eight Vasus are seen, O best of the Bharatas.
